description: Tenerife is the largest Canary Island, combining dramatic volcanic landscapes with year-round sunshine and a wide range of holiday styles. The south is defined by purpose-built resort strips with calm beaches, while the north is lush, cooler, and more authentically Spanish. Mount Teide, Spain's highest peak, dominates the interior and is a world-class hiking and stargazing destination.
climate: Subtropical year-round: south averages 22°C in winter and 28°C in summer; north is slightly cooler and occasionally cloudy. Sunshine almost every day.
geographic_note: Largest of the Canary Islands, located 300 km off the African coast; highest point is Mount Teide at 3,715 m.

description: Gran Canaria earns its nickname 'continent in miniature' with striking contrast between the golden sand dunes of Maspalomas in the south and misty pine forests inland. The south coast is one of Europe's top LGBTQ+ destinations, centred on Maspalomas and Playa del Inglés. The capital Las Palmas offers a cosmopolitan city experience with a beautiful urban beach.
climate: Subtropical year-round, very similar to Tenerife: warm and dry in the south, cooler and greener in the north. Trade winds keep summer temperatures comfortable.
geographic_note: Third largest Canary Island; Maspalomas dunes are a UNESCO biosphere reserve.

description: Fuerteventura is defined by its extraordinary beaches — long, wide, and uncrowded — and persistent trade winds that have made it one of Europe's premier windsurfing and kitesurfing destinations. The island has a raw, arid beauty with an unspoiled interior. It suits travellers seeking a natural beach escape rather than a built-up resort experience.
climate: Dry and warm year-round, cooled by constant trade winds. Among the sunniest Canary Islands; minimal rainfall. Sea temperatures remain comfortable even in winter.
geographic_note: Closest Canary Island to the African mainland; Sotavento beach hosts world-class windsurfing events annually.

description: Lanzarote is the most visually distinctive Canary Island, shaped by volcanic eruptions that created a surreal lunar landscape of black lava fields and fire mountains. Artist César Manrique left an indelible aesthetic mark — architecture blends into nature and overdevelopment has been resisted. Puerto del Carmen is the main resort strip; Playa Blanca is quieter and more upscale.
climate: Warm and dry year-round, often windier than other Canary Islands. Very little rainfall; reliable sunshine throughout the year.
geographic_note: Entire island is a UNESCO biosphere reserve; Timanfaya National Park protects the most dramatic lava fields.

description: Mallorca blends mass tourism in the south and east with dramatic mountains, cycling routes, and upscale retreats in the northwest. The Serra de Tramuntana mountains are UNESCO World Heritage; the south offers long sandy beaches and resort towns. Palma, the capital, is a sophisticated city with a Gothic cathedral and excellent gastronomy.
climate: Classic Mediterranean: hot, dry summers (28–32°C) and mild winters. Peak season is June–August; spring and autumn are pleasant with fewer crowds.
geographic_note: Largest Balearic Island; the Serra de Tramuntana is UNESCO World Heritage; Palma airport is one of Spain's busiest.

description: Ibiza is globally synonymous with world-class electronic music, superclubs, and vibrant nightlife, but also has a quieter bohemian side: hidden coves, organic farm restaurants, and the Dalt Vila UNESCO-listed old town. The north is increasingly popular for wellness retreats, yoga, and hippie-market culture. Beach clubs bridge both worlds.
climate: Hot Mediterranean summers (peak 30°C+) and mild winters. The best beach weather runs May–October.
geographic_note: Third largest Balearic Island; Dalt Vila old town is UNESCO World Heritage; home to some of the world's largest nightclubs.

description: Menorca is the quietest and most unspoiled Balearic Island, protected as a UNESCO Biosphere Reserve with strict limits on development. Its beaches — turquoise coves backed by pine forests — are among the most pristine in the Mediterranean. It suits travellers seeking tranquillity, natural beauty, and authentic local culture over resort strips and nightlife.
climate: Mediterranean with a twist: the Tramuntana wind from the north can be strong, especially in winter. Warm and reliable summers (26–28°C).
geographic_note: Smallest of the main Balearic Islands; entire island is a UNESCO biosphere reserve.

description: Costa Blanca is one of Spain's most popular resort coasts, centred on Benidorm — a Manhattan-shaped skyline on the sea that packs hotels, restaurants, and entertainment into a small area. Ideal for families and value-seeking couples with long sandy beaches and abundant amenities. Calpe and Altea offer quieter, more characterful alternatives.
climate: Among the sunniest coasts in Europe with over 300 sunny days annually. Warm summers (28–32°C) and mild winters averaging 15°C.
geographic_note: Stretches 200 km along the Alicante and Valencia coast; Benidorm is one of Europe's densest resort concentrations.

description: Costa del Sol is Andalusia's glittering Mediterranean coast, anchored by Marbella — a byword for upscale beach living, golf, and international glamour. The Golden Mile and Puerto Banús marina attract a wealthy international crowd, while Nerja and Frigiliana preserve whitewashed Moorish character. Málaga city provides cultural depth with the Picasso Museum and a thriving food scene.
climate: Warm Mediterranean: mild winters (around 16°C) and very hot summers (35°C+). The hottest and most reliably sunny stretch of mainland Spain's coastline.
geographic_note: 160 km coastline in Málaga Province; highest concentration of golf courses in Europe; Marbella's Golden Mile is internationally renowned.

description: The Algarve is Portugal's southern coast, famous for dramatic golden cliffs, hidden sea caves, and long sandy beaches backed by terracotta rock formations. It combines excellent surf beaches in the west with calmer family beaches in the east. Albufeira is the main resort town; Vilamoura is the golfing hub; Lagos and Sagres offer a rugged surf character.
climate: Warm Mediterranean with Atlantic influence: pleasant spring and autumn, hot summers (28–32°C), and mild winters. Receives some of Portugal's most abundant sunshine.
geographic_note: Southernmost province of Portugal; Praia da Marinha and Ponta da Piedade are among Europe's most photographed coastlines.

description: Madeira is a volcanic island rising dramatically from the Atlantic, carpeted in dense laurel forest (UNESCO World Heritage) and cut by levada irrigation channels that double as scenic hiking trails. Subtropical climate, dramatic scenery, and floral abundance set it apart from beach-focused islands. Funchal is a graceful capital with excellent restaurants and culture.
climate: Subtropical and mild year-round: never too hot (24°C max in summer) and rarely cold in winter. Rain falls mainly in the north; the south and Funchal are sheltered.
geographic_note: Portuguese archipelago 900 km southwest of Lisbon; no sandy beaches — swimming is at lido pools cut into volcanic rock.

description: Crete is Greece's largest island and a world in itself, with proud local culture, extraordinary Minoan archaeological sites, and landscapes from azure beach resorts to the rugged White Mountains. Heraklion and Chania are rewarding cultural cities; Elounda and Agios Nikolaos offer upscale resort experiences. Cretan food is widely considered the finest in Greece.
climate: Hot, dry Mediterranean summers (28–35°C); mild winters. Southern Crete has some of the longest sunshine hours in Greece.
geographic_note: Largest Greek island (8,336 km²); Minoan Palace of Knossos is one of Europe's oldest palace sites; Samaria Gorge is the longest gorge in Europe.

description: Rhodes combines a perfectly preserved medieval walled city (UNESCO World Heritage) with long sandy beaches and an energetic resort strip at Faliraki. Lindos in the south offers whitewashed village charm and an acropolis above a beautiful bay. It suits couples, families, and history enthusiasts, with lively but not overwhelming nightlife in Rhodes Town.
climate: Hot Mediterranean summers (28–32°C); very dry in summer; mild winters. One of Greece's most reliably sunny islands.
geographic_note: Largest Dodecanese island; medieval Old Town is UNESCO World Heritage; closest Greek island to Turkey (15 km).

description: Corfu is the greenest major Greek island, with Venetian-influenced architecture in Corfu Town, lush olive groves, and varied beaches from the lively Kavos strip in the south to quiet coves in the north. The British, French, and Venetian architectural legacy gives Corfu Town a uniquely cosmopolitan character. Paleokastritsa, with its turquoise coves, is one of the most beautiful spots in the Mediterranean.
climate: Mediterranean with more rainfall than most Greek islands, hence the lush vegetation. Warm summers (26–30°C) and mild winters.
geographic_note: Northernmost Ionian island, close to Albania and the Greek mainland; Corfu Town is a UNESCO World Heritage site.

description: Santorini is the most visually iconic Greek island, built on the rim of a submerged volcanic caldera. Famous blue-domed churches and whitewashed cliffs drop dramatically to the sea below. It is first and foremost a destination for couples — sunset views, boutique hotels, and excellent volcanic-soil wine. Crowded and expensive in peak season, but unmatched for romance.
climate: Hot and dry Mediterranean summer (26–30°C); mild winters. Sunshine is very reliable but the Meltemi wind can be strong in July–August.
geographic_note: Formed by one of history's largest volcanic eruptions (~1600 BCE); highest point is 566 m above the caldera; beaches are volcanic red and black sand.

description: Mykonos is Greece's most glamorous and internationally famous party island, known for its iconic windmills, super beach clubs, and a nightlife scene that attracts a global jet-set. It is also a major LGBTQ+ destination with a long tradition of inclusivity. Mykonos Town (Chora) is beautiful and navigable on foot. Outside peak season it becomes appreciably calmer and more affordable.
climate: Hot Mediterranean summer with the Meltemi wind reliably cooling things down in July–August (can disrupt ferries). Mild winters.
geographic_note: Most expensive Greek island; 33 km of coastline; accessible by ferry from Athens Piraeus in ~5 hours or by domestic flights.

description: Cyprus is the eastern Mediterranean's largest holiday island, offering ancient ruins at Paphos, sea caves and beach energy at Ayia Napa, and skiing on Troodos in winter. Ayia Napa on the east coast is a popular beach and party destination; Paphos on the west is more upscale and culturally rich. Dry heat, clear water, and long beaches make it ideal for sun seekers from spring through late autumn.
climate: Very hot and dry in summer (35°C+) with warm sea temperatures; mild and pleasant in spring and autumn; mild winters with some rain.
geographic_note: Third largest Mediterranean island; Aphrodite's legendary birthplace is near Paphos on the west coast; island divided since 1974.

description: Antalya is the gateway to Turkey's Turquoise Coast, with Belek offering some of Europe's finest golf courses alongside 5-star all-inclusive mega-resorts on long sandy beaches. The ancient old city (Kaleiçi) is a beautifully preserved Roman–Ottoman quarter. Perge, Aspendos, and Side are easily reached ruins. Turkish hospitality and exceptional value for money are consistent highlights.
climate: Very hot Mediterranean summers (35–38°C) and mild winters. One of Turkey's hottest summer destinations; shoulder seasons are ideal for sightseeing.
geographic_note: Antalya Province hosts more tourists than any other region in Turkey; Belek is a designated special tourism zone with 20+ golf courses.

description: Bodrum is Turkey's most cosmopolitan resort — a whitewashed town on a promontory with a famous medieval castle and a marina packed with gulets and superyachts. Marmaris, further along the Muğla coast, is wilder and more active, with a large marina and easy access to Greek islands. Both attract international visitors with an upscale trend in Bodrum Town.
climate: Very hot and dry in summer (35°C+) and mild in winter. Bodrum's sheltered bays can be calmer than more exposed Turkish coasts.
geographic_note: Site of the ancient Mausoleum of Halicarnassus (one of the Seven Wonders); 15 km from the Greek island of Kos.

description: The Amalfi Coast is one of the world's most celebrated coastal landscapes: 50 km of cliffside towns, lemon groves, and azure coves between Positano and Salerno. Positano is the most photographed village — a vertical cascade of pastel houses with a pebbly beach below. The coast is aspirational and relatively expensive, naturally suiting honeymooners, couples, and lovers of Italian culture.
climate: Warm Mediterranean summers (26–30°C) with moderate humidity; mild winters. The narrow coastal road and crowds make visiting most comfortable in May, June, or September.
geographic_note: UNESCO World Heritage landscape; the SS163 Amalfitana is one of the world's most scenic coastal drives but extremely narrow.

description: Sardinia is Italy's second-largest island, known for extraordinary beaches — turquoise water, white sand, and dramatically clear visibility that rivals the Caribbean. Porto Cervo and the Costa Smeralda in the northeast have long been an ultra-luxury enclave. The interior is wild, mountainous, and culturally distinct, preserving a unique Nuragic civilisation heritage.
climate: Hot, dry Mediterranean summers (28–32°C) and mild winters. Mistral wind can make spring and autumn pleasantly cool or uncomfortably windy.
geographic_note: Costa Smeralda was developed by the Aga Khan in the 1960s as a private luxury enclave; La Pelosa beach near Stintino is considered one of Italy's finest.

description: Dubrovnik's perfectly preserved Renaissance city walls enclose a marble-paved old town on the Adriatic, making it one of Europe's most beautiful cities. It gained additional global fame as the filming location for King's Landing in Game of Thrones. Boat excursions reach the Elaphiti islands and Montenegro. It suits cultural travellers, couples, and history enthusiasts.
climate: Mediterranean with hot summers (28–32°C), plenty of sunshine, and mild winters. Summers can be crowded and sweltering; spring and autumn are generally preferable.
geographic_note: UNESCO World Heritage city; city walls are 1,940 m long and up to 25 m high; Lokrum island is 10 minutes by ferry.

description: Hvar is the sunniest and arguably most glamorous Croatian island, with a chic harbour town, lavender fields, and a sophisticated beach club and nightlife scene that attracts a younger international crowd. The Pakleni Islands offshore are a kayaker's and sailor's paradise of clear coves. The interior and south coast are quieter and more authentically Croatian.
climate: One of the sunniest places in Europe; hot summers (28–32°C) and mild winters. Very dry in summer with reliable sunshine.
geographic_note: Claims 2,724 sunshine hours per year — among the highest in Europe; accessible by catamaran from Split; no cars in Hvar Town.

description: Marrakech is a sensory overload in the best sense: a medieval medina of winding souks, ornate riads, and Djemaa el-Fna square — one of the world's great public spaces. Beyond the city, the High Atlas mountains are visible and accessible. Luxury riad hotels offer intimate contrast to the bustling streets. It rewards those seeking culture, colour, and adventure rather than a beach holiday.
climate: Semi-arid: very hot in summer (35–42°C); pleasantly warm in spring and autumn (18–25°C); cool winters. Minimal rainfall year-round.
geographic_note: UNESCO World Heritage medina; Djemaa el-Fna is UNESCO Intangible Cultural Heritage; High Atlas peak Toubkal (4,167 m) is 70 km away.

description: Agadir is Morocco's purpose-built beach resort — a modern, open city with a 10 km arc of sandy Atlantic beach and a laid-back atmosphere very different from the intensity of Marrakech or Fez. Wind conditions on the beach make it excellent for surfing and kitesurfing. It suits travellers wanting a relaxed Morocco beach holiday without a busy medina experience.
climate: Excellent year-round: warm but rarely oppressive thanks to Atlantic breezes. Winters are mild (18–20°C); summers warm but comfortable (24–28°C).
geographic_note: Rebuilt after a 1960 earthquake; the 10 km beach is the widest in Morocco; Anti-Atlas mountains are visible inland.

description: Barbados is the Caribbean's most refined and culturally rich island, combining world-class sandy beaches with a sophisticated food and drinks scene and a proud Bajan culture. The west coast (Platinum Coast) has the calmest water and most exclusive hotels; the east coast is wild and surf-battered. The most British-influenced Caribbean island, giving it particular accessibility for UK travellers.
climate: Warm and tropical year-round (26–30°C); trade winds keep it comfortable. Hurricane season is June–November, but Barbados sits south of the main hurricane belt.
geographic_note: Easternmost Caribbean island; became a republic in 2021; birthplace of Rihanna; home to Mount Gay, the world's oldest rum brand.

description: Cancún is the Americas' most visited beach resort — a 20 km hotel zone of all-inclusive mega-resorts on brilliant white Caribbean sand. The Yucatán Peninsula's cenotes, Mayan ruins at Chichén Itzá and Tulum, and the Mesoamerican Barrier Reef make extraordinary day trips. Warm water year-round and energetic nightlife make it a favourite for families and young adults alike.
climate: Tropical: warm year-round (28–32°C) with high humidity. Rainy season is June–October with afternoon storms and hurricane risk; December–April is ideal.
geographic_note: Caribbean shore of Mexico's Yucatán Peninsula; Mesoamerican Barrier Reef (world's second largest) runs the length of the coast.

description: The Maldives defines the fantasy of island paradise: overwater bungalows on stilts above a turquoise lagoon, white sand islands barely a metre above sea level, and some of the world's finest coral reefs. The ultimate destination for honeymooners, divers, and those seeking complete seclusion and luxury. Almost all resorts are on private islands; the experience is deliberately exclusive.
climate: Tropical year-round (28–32°C); the northeast monsoon (December–April) brings the dry, calm-sea season; the southwest monsoon (May–November) brings rain and choppier seas.
geographic_note: Lowest-elevation nation on earth (average 1.5 m above sea level); 1,192 islands in 26 atolls.

description: Phuket is Thailand's largest island and most developed beach destination, offering a spectrum from the backpacker energy of Patong Beach to the quieter, upscale bays of Kata, Karon, and Surin. It serves as a gateway to the limestone karst islands of Phang Nga Bay and the Similan Islands for diving. Thai food, spa culture, and exceptional value relative to European standards are consistent attractions.
climate: Tropical monsoon: dry season November–April (the ideal holiday period); wet season May–October with heavy rain and reduced sea visibility.
geographic_note: Connected to mainland Thailand by two bridges; day trips to James Bond Island in Phang Nga Bay are iconic.

description: Koh Samui is Thailand's second most visited island — calmer and greener than Phuket, with a circular ring road linking coconut-palm beaches, luxury resorts, and a growing wellness and yoga scene. Chaweng is the most active beach; Bo Phut fisherman's village is charming and relaxed. The Full Moon Party on Koh Phangan is a short ferry ride away.
climate: Tropical, but Samui's weather differs from Phuket: dry season runs roughly February–September; October–January can be wet and stormy (Gulf of Thailand side).
geographic_note: Gulf of Thailand island in Surat Thani Province; accessible by direct flights from Bangkok; Koh Tao and Koh Phangan are nearby by ferry.
